courseEvidence.name: Personal & Professional Development
courseEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courseEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
courseEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courseEvidence.contribution: Academic writing and literature synthesis

courseEvidence.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
courseEvidence.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
courseEvidence.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments
courseEvidence.contribution: Molecules, cells and organ-system foundation

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Programming
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
courseEvidence.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
courseEvidence.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling
courseEvidence.contribution: Python programming and debugging

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Data Science
courseEvidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
courseEvidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
courseEvidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Data cleaning and visualization

courseEvidence.name: Mathematical Methods
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
courseEvidence.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
courseEvidence.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Calculus, linear algebra and differential equations

courseEvidence.name: Neurobiology
courseEvidence.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
courseEvidence.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders
courseEvidence.contribution: Comparative neuroanatomy and microscopy

courseEvidence.name: Functional Anatomy
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Skeletal, thoracic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, reproductive and lower urinary anatomy are developed through spatial reasoning, medical images, anatomical drawing and human-specimen material. Guided practicals and dissection-room observation connect three-dimensional relationships to variation. Historical, ethical and societal questions about human remains, representation and sex accompany the anatomical study; activities are framed as academic learning rather than clinical qualification.
courseEvidence.topics: Anatomical terminology and body planes; Medical imaging; Skeletal system and vertebral column; Thorax and pelvis; Respiratory and cardiovascular systems; Abdominal organs and vascular supply; Reproductive and lower urinary systems; Anatomical variation and intersex presentations; Human remains and dissection ethics; History and representation of the body
courseEvidence.methods: Surface-anatomy observation; Anatomical image interpretation; Scientific anatomical drawing; Three-dimensional anatomical reasoning; Guided study of human skeletal remains and anatomical specimens; Ethical reflection on anatomical practice
courseEvidence.contribution: Anatomical imaging interpretation and dissection materials

courseEvidence.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courseEvidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
courseEvidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
courseEvidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Measurement, research design and inference

courseEvidence.name: Human Physiology
courseEvidence.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
courseEvidence.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
courseEvidence.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision
courseEvidence.contribution: Homeostasis and organ function

courseEvidence.name: Biochemistry
courseEvidence.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
courseEvidence.topics: Water and weak bonds; Amino acids and protein structure; Protein-biochemistry techniques; Enzyme action, kinetics, regulation and inhibition; Hemoglobin; Carbohydrates and lipids; Metabolic organization; Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; Glycogen and pentose-phosphate metabolism; Fatty-acid and lipid metabolism; Nitrogen and urea cycle; Biochemical mechanisms of disease
courseEvidence.methods: Biochemical pathway and disease-mechanism analysis; Primary-literature review
courseEvidence.contribution: Biomolecule structure, enzymes and metabolism

courseEvidence.name: Pharmacology
courseEvidence.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies how drugs act at molecular, cellular and whole-body levels and how the body handles them. Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics provide foundations for rational therapies and drug-target identification. Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.
courseEvidence.topics: Drug discovery and targets; Drug-receptor interactions; Pharmacodynamics; Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination; Pharmacokinetics; Antimicrobial therapy; Inflammation and immunopharmacology; Autonomic regulation; Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Pharmacogenomics; Drug toxicity; Access to experimental treatments and evidence; Homeopathy
courseEvidence.methods: Concentration-response modelling; Pharmacokinetic time-concentration and time-response analysis; Pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameter calculation; Virtual organ-bath experiments; Hypothesis and experimental-design development
courseEvidence.contribution: Dose response and pharmacokinetic modeling

courseEvidence.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
courseEvidence.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
courseEvidence.profile: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
courseEvidence.topics: Cell injury, adaptation and death; Acute and chronic inflammation; Regeneration, repair and fibrosis; Neoplasia; Pulmonary pathology; Leukemia and lymphoma; Genes, genomes and inheritance; Genetic variation and chromosome abnormalities; Gene regulation and epigenetics; Genotype-phenotype relationships; Genetic testing and DNA technologies; Gene-based therapies and cell manipulation; Genetics ethics, law and biosafety
courseEvidence.methods: Biomedical literature review; Research-grant proposal design; Hypothesis formulation and experimental-control selection; Research feasibility, timeline and budget planning; Stakeholder-based ethical argument analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Genetic testing, pathology and research proposal design

courseEvidence.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops numerical solutions to mathematical problems that lack convenient analytical solutions, emphasizing when algorithms work and how to validate their output. Students study numerical root finding, interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, ordinary differential equations, and linear and nonlinear systems. Mathematica notebooks apply and compare textbook algorithms with built-in routines, with attention to roundoff, convergence, error, stability and sensitivity.
courseEvidence.topics: Computer arithmetic and roundoff; Algorithm convergence and error; Scalar root finding; Polynomial interpolation and splines; Parametric curves; Numerical differentiation and integration; Initial-value problems; Multistep and adaptive differential-equation methods; Stability and stiff equations; Linear systems and matrix factorization; Nonlinear systems; Numerical-result validation
courseEvidence.methods: Mathematica numerical computation; Bisection, fixed-point, Newton and secant methods; Polynomial and spline interpolation; Numerical differentiation and Richardson extrapolation; Simpson, Romberg and Gaussian quadrature; Adaptive quadrature; Euler and Runge-Kutta methods; Multistep predictor-corrector methods; Gaussian elimination and pivoting; Matrix factorizations; Newton and quasi-Newton methods for systems; Steepest descent; Continuation methods
courseEvidence.contribution: Numerical approximation and differential equations

courseEvidence.name: Molecular Cell Biology
courseEvidence.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
courseEvidence.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
courseEvidence.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Cell function, molecular mechanisms and free-energy calculations

courseEvidence.name: Mechanisms of Disease
courseEvidence.description2: Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.
courseEvidence.profile: Connects normal organ function to pathophysiology across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Students integrate anatomy and physiology to explain symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnostic findings, treatment and prognosis. Published clinical cases develop differential reasoning and appraisal of diagnostic procedures. A creative assignment constructs an imaginary disease whose symptoms, mechanism and proposed treatment must form a coherent pathophysiological account.
courseEvidence.topics: Organ-system disease mechanisms; Nutrition and digestive disease; Hematological and cardiovascular disease; Respiratory disease; Renal failure, dialysis and transplantation; Endocrine disorders; Neurological disease; Etiology and pathogenesis; Diagnosis, treatment and prognosis; Medical ethics; Rheumatic disease
courseEvidence.methods: Clinical case analysis; Differential diagnosis reasoning; Critical appraisal of diagnostic and laboratory procedures; Integration of anatomy, physiology and clinical evidence; Mechanistic modelling of an imaginary disease; Biomedical literature comparison
courseEvidence.contribution: Clinical case analysis and disease mechanisms

courseEvidence.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
courseEvidence.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
courseEvidence.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
courseEvidence.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design
courseEvidence.contribution: Neural networks and computer vision

courseEvidence.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
courseEvidence.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
courseEvidence.topics: Disease frequency and risk; Incidence and prevalence; Measures of association; Epidemiological study designs; Bias, confounding and causality; Outbreak investigation; Social and environmental health determinants; Health inequalities; Health promotion; Health-needs assessment; Screening; Evidence-informed interventions and implementation
courseEvidence.methods: Epidemiological rate and risk calculation; Descriptive and analytic epidemiology; Study-design and evidence appraisal; Population-health data interpretation; Outbreak analysis; Health-needs assessment; Stakeholder interviewing; Evidence-informed intervention development
courseEvidence.contribution: Study design and screening at population scale

courseEvidence.name: Machine Learning
courseEvidence.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
courseEvidence.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
courseEvidence.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation
courseEvidence.contribution: Prediction and cross-validation

courseEvidence.name: Linear Algebra
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
courseEvidence.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
courseEvidence.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation
courseEvidence.contribution: Linear systems, Fourier series and discrete signals

courseEvidence.name: Probability & Statistics
courseEvidence.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
courseEvidence.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
courseEvidence.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
courseEvidence.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica
courseEvidence.contribution: Probability models and inference

courseEvidence.name: Infection & Immunity
courseEvidence.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines host-microbe interactions and the immune mechanisms that protect against infection or cause disease. Microbiology and innate defence lead into antibodies, antigen recognition, lymphocyte development and memory, effector responses and mucosal immunity. Vaccination, allergy, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity connect mechanisms to clinical problems. Students analyze lymphocyte phenotypes using original flow-cytometry data and synthesize recent research in an extended and graphical abstract.
courseEvidence.topics: Infectious agents and microbial virulence; Host defence and immune evasion; Immune cells, organs and cytokines; Innate immunity and complement; Antibodies and antigen recognition; MHC and lymphocyte receptors; Lymphocyte activation, development and memory; Cell- and antibody-mediated immunity; Mucosal immunity; Vaccination and viral infections; Hypersensitivity and allergy; Immunodeficiency; Autoimmune disease; Outbreak management
courseEvidence.methods: Flow-cytometry data analysis and lymphocyte phenotyping; Clinical symptom and mechanism analysis; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Critical analysis of immunological research; Graphical synthesis of scientific findings
courseEvidence.contribution: Flow cytometry interpretation and immune mechanisms

courseEvidence.name: Life Science Laboratory
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
courseEvidence.profile: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
courseEvidence.topics: Blood cells and proteins; Blood groups and hemograms; Aseptic culture and bacterial identification; Disinfection and sterilization; Antibiotic susceptibility; Genetically modified bacteria; GFP production and purification; DNA and plasmid analysis; PCR and restriction digestion; Protein and DNA databases; Genotype and population-genetic interpretation; Experimental reproducibility
courseEvidence.methods: Pipetting and workflow planning; Microscopy and blood-smear examination; Blood cell counting and hemogram measurement; ELISA; Aseptic culture and purity streaking; Bacterial identification and inhibition-zone testing; Sterilization and disinfection testing; pGLO bacterial transformation; Protein extraction and chromatographic purification; SDS-PAGE; DNA and plasmid isolation; PCR; Restriction digestion and agarose-gel electrophoresis; DNA and protein database searching; Laboratory notebook and scientific-report preparation
courseEvidence.contribution: Molecular wet-lab work including ELISA, PCR and introductory bioinformatics

courseEvidence.name: Database Management Systems
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
courseEvidence.contribution: Database design and queries

courseEvidence.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
courseEvidence.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
courseEvidence.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
courseEvidence.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images
courseEvidence.contribution: Image filtering and segmentation, including medical examples

courseEvidence.name: Sustainability Essentials I
courseEvidence.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
courseEvidence.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
courseEvidence.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
courseEvidence.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement
courseEvidence.contribution: Chemical equilibrium, energy and dynamic systems in sustainability

courseEvidence.name: Sustainability Essentials II
courseEvidence.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
courseEvidence.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
courseEvidence.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
courseEvidence.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design
courseEvidence.contribution: Oscilloscope wave analysis, optical spectroscopy, microscopy and chemical testing

courseEvidence.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
courseEvidence.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
courseEvidence.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
courseEvidence.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations
courseEvidence.contribution: Electrochemical recovery, ICP metal analysis and scanning electron microscopy

courseEvidence.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry
courseEvidence.description2: Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering, mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises geochemical modelling and a case study.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines chemical and biological controls on near-surface Earth systems, especially interactions among water, minerals, rocks and soils. Students study aqueous composition, equilibrium, speciation, carbonate and redox chemistry, adsorption, weathering and biomineralization. Laboratory investigations and geochemical modelling connect these processes to contaminant behaviour, wastewater treatment, remediation and resource recovery. A project applies geochemical principles to a current environmental issue.
courseEvidence.topics: Natural-water composition; Chemical equilibrium and ionic activity; Aqueous speciation and complexation; Mineral saturation, precipitation and dissolution; Carbonate equilibria, alkalinity and buffering; Ocean acidification; Redox processes and microbial controls; Adsorption and mineral surfaces; Weathering and clay formation; Biomineralization; Contaminant transport; Environmental remediation and resource recovery
courseEvidence.methods: Geochemical equilibrium and speciation modelling; Geochemist's Workbench; Piper diagrams; Pourbaix and stability diagrams; Laboratory geochemical investigations; Geochemical data interpretation
courseEvidence.contribution: Chemical equilibrium and lab geochemistry reinforce analytical reasoning but are directed at natural waters and mineral systems.

courseEvidence.name: Soils & Aquifers
courseEvidence.description2: Explores soils and aquifers through fieldwork and lab analyses. Covers soil formation, properties, health and remediation and investigates mapping aquifers for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater resource assessment.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines soils and shallow aquifers through soil science, environmental chemistry and applied geophysics. Soil formation, functions, quality and threats connect to texture, structure, composition, biological activity and salinization. Field sampling and laboratory investigations characterize soil properties and sediment-cell behaviour. Seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers. Students document procedures and observations, process field data in Excel, interpret results and develop evidence-based field and laboratory reports.
courseEvidence.topics: Soil formation, functions and taxonomy; Soil quality, amendments and threats; Soil texture, structure and aggregate stability; Soil moisture and organic matter; Soil chemistry, pH and metals; Soil biology; Sediment-cell behaviour; Shallow aquifers, salinization and freshwater interventions; Physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers; Seismology; Electrical resistivity; Electromagnetic surveying
courseEvidence.methods: Soil coring and field sampling; Visual soil-structure assessment (grass-VESS); Aggregate-stability, texture and sieve tests; Soil pH, moisture, organic-content and leaching analyses; Microscopy and SEM-EDS; Sample preparation for ICP/IC and interpretation of ICP results; Methylene-blue testing with spectrophotometry/titration; Seismic surveying; Electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveying; Field-data processing in Excel
courseEvidence.contribution: pH, leaching and soils laboratory work uses environmental samples and does not train clinical assay design.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
courseEvidence.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
courseEvidence.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
courseEvidence.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Neural signaling and brain anatomy support biological interpretation without instrument acquisition training.

courseEvidence.name: Media Archaeology
courseEvidence.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
courseEvidence.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
courseEvidence.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research
courseEvidence.contribution: Hands-on media technologies include historical optics but do not supply quantitative optics or medical measurement progression.

comparability.label: Biomedical Science and Health Data Science
comparability.reason: A feasible 24-course sequence covers physiology, disease mechanisms, experimental molecular biology, probability, image processing and prediction. Interpreting and processing medical images contributes to diagnostics, while the sequence lacks depth in how instruments acquire the underlying measurements.

comparability.label: Medical physics reconstruction through sustainability and computation
comparability.reason: A second feasible 24-course sequence combines physics and chemistry in Sustainability Essentials I and II with R3 instrumentation and biochemical laboratory work. Optical spectroscopy, Fourier wave analysis, electron microscopy, electrochemical recovery and instrument-based materials analysis provide genuine technical overlap. The applications and later progression remain in sustainability and materials, with no sustained experimental medical-physics or clinical analytical-chemistry sequence.

comparability.label: Molecular diagnostics and bioinformatics
comparability.reason: Life Science Laboratory, molecular pathology and cell biology provide meaningful molecular diagnostics and introductory bioinformatics, supported by computing and mathematics. They do not establish a sequence in biological network dynamics, sequence and transcriptomics analysis, or measured physiological signal modeling.

repair: Swap Neural Networks & Deep Learning and Infection & Immunity in the biomedical plan. The physical methods reconstruction replaces Neurobiology, Epidemiology & Public Health and Databases with Sustainability Essentials I and II and R3, retaining physiology, biochemistry, molecular lab and image analysis. The alternatives test different emphasis and overlap extensively. Neither yields a comparable progression in experimental medical physics and clinical analytical chemistry.
